title: Silent Checks
story: The auditor wants proof that someone actually reads the health checks. They report the way monitoring tools do: exit status 0 means healthy and anything else means trouble. Some of them also chat on the way out, which proves nothing either way.
objective: Run the health checks in /opt/checks and record the name of each failing check (api for api.sh) in /reports/failing-checks.txt, one per line in alphabetical order.
hints: A check's verdict is its exit status, not its output. Run one, then echo $? to see 0 for success or a non-zero failure status.
Command lists act on that status: a && b runs b only when a succeeds, and a || b runs b only when a fails.
Append with >> so each failing name adds a line instead of replacing the file, and work through the checks alphabetically.
Try: ./api.sh || echo api >> /reports/failing-checks.txt, then repeat it for cert, disk, and queue.
explanation: Automation reads exit statuses, not prose. A script's status is the status of its last command, so each check passes or fails on its final grep -q. echo $? shows the most recent status, a || b turns a failure into an action, and a && b continues only after success. The output was a decoy: the certificate warning came from a passing check, and the queue's cheerful message came from a failing one.

files.content:
#!/bin/sh
# Healthy while the certificate is valid; renewal reminders are only warnings.
echo 'WARNING: certificate renews in 45 days'
grep -q '^valid=yes$' /var/state/cert.state

#!/bin/sh
# Healthy when the work queue is empty.
echo 'queue check finished'
grep -q '^backlog=0$' /var/state/queue.state
